answer.rationale:
The inherited memory most likely to drive an aggressive move is memory_c2 (a full switch to the low-cost vendor cut unit cost with quick onboarding). Before acting on it I want the original record, because the current conditions differ in the one way that matters: the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. If c2's switch happened with slack capacity, a long qualification runway, or on a less critical component, it does not license a hard cutover here — an unqualified primary at zero buffer converts a cost win into a delivery failure, which the objective forbids. I also want memory_c6 verified, because it names the only lever not yet exhausted this cycle: the incumbent refused to reopen price, but c6 says a multi-year volume commitment cut unit cost without narrowing scope. That is a structurally different negotiation than the one that was refused, and it is compatible with memory_c4's benchmarking result. So my intent is to negotiate terms — pursuing volume/term-based pricing plus a short bridge extension to remove the 14-day cliff — rather than switch primary supply, and to keep the commitment small and guarded rather than locking a long multi-year deal on one cycle's pressure.

Uncertainty I am explicitly not resolving: I do not know that negotiation will reach the full 18%. It may land short, and the honest read is that the mandate may not be fully satisfiable this cycle without taking delivery risk. Two downstream risks I am flagging rather than burying. First, a multi-year lock-in bought under a cost mandate narrows future optionality and weakens leverage at the next review — c6 records the price benefit but says nothing about what the longer term cost in flexibility. Second, the real durable fix is memory_c3's dual-source pattern: qualifying the low-cost vendor on a limited share while the incumbent carries volume would capture much of the savings and remove the single point of failure, but it needs qualification lead time that 14 days and 94% utilization do not allow. I am deliberately sequencing: buy time and price now, then dual-source at the next review with the low-cost vendor's quote as the benchmark. If verification shows c2's switch was in fact done under tight capacity on a comparable part, or shows c6's volume pricing was contingent on terms Halden cannot now offer, I will revisit toward switch_primary_vendor or a staged second source instead.
